report:
Based on this research, here's my assessment of the evidence:

## Conclusion: The evidence supports "yes" — but with important nuance

Regular intake of cranberry juice or cranberry extract **does modestly reduce the risk of recurrent cystitis/UTIs in women**, particularly those with a history of recurrent infections, though the effect is not dramatic and depends heavily on the product's proanthocyanidin (PAC) content.

## The Evidence

**Cochrane systematic review (updated 2023)** — the gold-standard evidence source, pooling 50 randomized controlled trials with 8,857 participants. It found cranberry products significantly reduced UTI risk overall (roughly 25–30% relative reduction), with the strongest and most consistent benefit specifically in **women with recurrent UTIs**, as well as in children and people undergoing certain urologic procedures. Notably, benefit was *not* demonstrated in elderly institutionalized adults, pregnant women, or those with neurogenic bladder dysfunction — indicating the effect is population-specific (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321_cranberries-preventing-urinary-tract-infections).

**Mechanism**: Cranberries contain A-type proanthocyanidins that inhibit adhesion of P-fimbriated uropathogenic *E. coli* (the main cause of UTIs) to bladder urothelial cells, preventing colonization rather than killing bacteria — explaining plausibility without promoting antibiotic resistance (https://www.dovepress.com/cranberry-products-in-the-prevention-of-urinary-tract-infections-exami-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-BTAT).

**Dose-dependency**: Research indicates PAC concentration matters — trials using standardized, higher-PAC formulations show more consistent effects than low-dose juices, explaining inconsistency across older studies (https://cobfoundation.org/health-information/cranberry-vs-d-mannose-for-uti-prevention/).

## Caveat
This is prevention, not treatment — cranberry does not treat an active infection, and effect sizes are modest, not a replacement for antibiotics in high-risk cases.
